question_en: Tax loss carryforwards are best described as losses in the current year that:
explanation_en:
Deferred tax assets (DTAs) and liabilities (DTLs) are created to help reconcile temporary differences between tax expense and taxes payable.
Differences can occur because:
tax expense is derived from net income based on accounting standards, whereas
taxes payable is derived from taxable income based on the tax code.
A DTA is created when a company reports higher revenues or lower expenses for tax purposes than it reports on its financial statements. When
this happens, taxes payable are greater than tax expenses for the period (ie, the company pays more tax earlier and less later). A DTL occurs in
the reverse situation.
Tax loss carryforwards, a type of DTA, occur when the absolute value of accounting losses is greater than the current year's taxable income.
Subject to local tax laws, accounting losses offset taxable income. Since the tax benefit (lowering taxable income and, thus, taxes payable) from
losses is allowed only to the extent of the current year's taxable income, losses exceeding that amount are carried forward to offset future taxable
income. This excess portion of the loss, which will provide a future tax benefit, is a DTA since the company may reduce taxes payable in the
future.
(Choice A) Carryforwards create DTAs, not DTLs, since the company gets the benefit of lower taxes in the future.
(Choice C) Carryforwards create DTAs that can offset future, not past, tax obligations.

question_en: An analyst gathers the following information about a company that reports under US GAAP: In Year 2, the decrease in net deferred tax assets most likely results from an increase in:
explanation_en:
Deferred tax assets (DTA) and liabilities (DTL) result from temporary differences between taxable income (based on tax reporting) and
accounting profit (based on financial reporting).
DTA are created when companies pay higher current taxes since taxable income is greater than accounting profit. This creates future tax
benefits, as in this scenario.
DTL are created when companies pay lower current taxes since taxable income is less than accounting profit. This creates future tax
liabilities.
The carrying amount of DTA represents the recoverable tax benefit, so if a company does not expect to generate enough taxable income to fully
recover the DTA, it must reduce the carrying amount. In that case, under US GAAP a company would create or increase a valuation allowance,
which is a contra account that decreases DTA. Under IFRS, the company reduces DTA directly and does not use a valuation allowance.
DTL and DTA (net of the valuation allowance) are combined and presented as net DTA (DTL) on the balance sheet. Therefore, an increase in the
valuation allowance would result in a decrease in the net DTA reported.
(Choice A) An increase in statutory tax rates would increase net DTA.
(Choice C) Since taxable income exceeds accounting profit in Year 2, there is an increase in DTA, not DTL.

question_en: The value of deferred tax liabilities is most likely based on tax rates:
option_a: as of the balance sheet date.
option_b: averaged over the current fiscal year.
option_c: expected to apply when the liability is satisfied.
explanation_en:
Deferred tax asset vs. deferred tax liability
Item created Accounting reporting Tax reporting
Deferred tax asset1 Income tax expense < Taxes payable
Deferred tax liability2 Income tax expense > Taxes payable
1Overpayment of tax in current period creates deferred tax asset
2Underpayment of tax in current period creates deferred tax liability
Deferred taxes account for temporary differences between income tax expense and taxes payable. Such differences occur due to differences
between tax reporting and financial reporting. A deferred tax liability (DTL) is created when a company pays less tax (tax reporting) than it reports
on its income statement (financial reporting); the DTL represents future taxes payable.
While current taxes payable are based on the tax rates that apply on the balance sheet date, a DTL is measured by tax rates that are expected
to be in place at the time of the liability's settlement. If expected rates are higher or lower than existing rates, that will be reflected in the value of
the DTL. This provides a more realistic measure of value since it is based on future rates, not historical ones (eg, balance sheet date, average
over the fiscal year) (Choices A and B).

question_en: Which of the following most likely creates a deferred tax asset?
option_a: Carryforward of prior years' gains, offset by current losses
option_b: Greater expenses for financial reporting than for tax reporting
option_c: Foreign currency received for income earned during the same period
explanation_en:
Comparison of deferred tax assets (DTA) and liabilities (DTL)
DTA DTL
Temporary
Taxable income > accounting income Taxable income < accounting income
differences
Future tax
Decrease Increase
obligations
Revaluation Change value if future earnings are at risk None
Accelerated for financial reporting; straight-line for tax Straight-line for financial reporting; accelerated for tax
Depreciation
reporting reporting
Expenses Expenses recorded before cash is paid Expenses recorded after cash is paid
Carryforwards Prior years' losses None
Revenue Cash received before revenue is earned Cash received after revenue is earned
A deferred tax asset (DTA) is created when a company's accounting income is less than its taxable income. In that case, according to the tax
code, the tax expense that the company must pay is greater than its income tax expense based on financial reporting. Often, these differences
arise when the tax code and accounting standards differ on how and when companies should recognize revenues and expenses. A DTA is
temporary since its benefit is expected to offset future taxes.
For example, accounting income is less than taxable income when a company elects accelerated depreciation for financial reporting and straight-
line depreciation for tax reporting. Using straight-line depreciation for tax reporting results in lower depreciation expense and higher taxable
income than when it is used for financial reporting. Higher taxable income increases tax expense and taxes payable. Overpayment of tax today
results in a DTA since the company will pay less tax in the future.
(Choice A) Carryforwards of prior years' losses, not gains, may be used against future gains and are recorded as DTAs. Under most tax laws,
gains are immediately taxable and are usually disallowed as carryforwards.
(Choice C) Foreign or domestic currency received for revenue earned during the same period creates neither a DTA nor a deferred tax liability
since accounting standards and the tax code recognize the currency as income.

question_en: A company reports the following information in its first year of operations: All else equal, if the tax rate had been 25% instead of 20%, then most likely the company's:
option_a: deferred tax assets would have been €750 lower.
option_b: deferred tax assets would have been €750 higher.
option_c: deferred tax liabilities would have been €750 higher.
explanation_en:
Deferred tax assets (DTA) and liabilities arise from temporary differences between income tax expense and taxes payable for a period. These
differences are expected to reverse over time and offset previous deferred tax items. Income tax expense is based on reported accounting
income from the income statement. Taxes payable is based on taxable income on the tax return and is the actual amount owed to the
government.
DTA arise when:
Taxable income > Accounting income and
Taxes payable > Tax expense.
Deferred tax liabilities (DTL) arise when:
Taxable income < Accounting income and
Taxes payable < Tax expense.
In this scenario, a DTA is created since taxable income is greater than accounting income (Choice C).
The deferred tax amount can be calculated as the product of the absolute difference between the taxable income and accounting income and the
tax rate. Therefore, the size of the deferred tax item is directly correlated to the tax rate. If the tax rate were higher, the amount of the DTA
increase would be higher as well (Choice A).

question_en: A company that reports under US GAAP has recognized a change in both deferred tax assets and deferred tax liabilities from the previous year. This year its taxes payable decreases and it reports a higher tax expense. The most likely reason this occurred is that:
option_c: the company uses straight-line depreciation for financial and tax reporting.
explanation_en:
The equation above demonstrates the relationship between taxes payable, tax expense, deferred tax liabilities (DTL) and deferred tax assets
(DTA). Here, tax expense increases, but taxes payable decreases. Rearranging the equation produces:
Higher tax expense and lower taxes payable make the left side of the equation larger. To maintain equality, the right side must increase as well,
which occurs when deferred tax liabilities (DTL) increase from the previous year (ie, the change in DTL is positive) and/or deferred tax assets
(DTA) decrease from the previous year (ie, the change in DTA is negative).
DTA offset future taxes, but the company must reasonably expect to generate future taxes that the DTA can offset. If that is not the case and the
DTA is less likely to be used, then:
under US GAAP, a valuation allowance is established to show the reduced value of the DTA.

question_en: In 20X0, a company's deferred tax liabilities increased by €3 million and its deferred tax assets decreased by €2 million. If the company reports €80 million in taxes payable, then its income tax expense (in € millions) is closest to:
explanation_en:
Deferred tax assets (DTA) and deferred tax liabilities (DTL) reflect temporary differences between income tax expense and taxes payable for a
period. Such differences are created by differences between accounting standards and tax laws. Income tax expense is reported on the income
statement according to accounting standards, whereas taxes payable is the actual amount owed to the government based on applicable tax laws.
When tax expense is greater than taxes payable, a DTL is created since the company pays less in taxes in the current period but will owe
more in taxes in the future.
When tax expense is less than taxes payable, a DTA is created since the company pays more in taxes in the current period and will owe
less in taxes in the future.
The equation above shows how changes in DTL and DTA are related to tax expense and taxes payable. To calculate tax expense in this scenario,
substitute the values for all of the other variables.
Tax expense = Taxes payable + ΔDTL – ΔDTA = 80 + 3 – (-2) = 85
(Choice A) 79 results from incorrectly subtracting the change in DTL and adding the change in DTA to taxes payable.
(Choice B) 81 results from incorrectly adding the change in DTA.

question_en: For a company reporting under US GAAP, nontaxable income generated from holding municipal bonds most likely causes:
option_a: a valuation allowance created for certain deferred tax assets.
option_b: a temporary difference between taxable profit and accounting profit.
option_c: a permanent difference between taxable profit and accounting profit.
explanation_en:
Major areas resulting in permanent differences between pretax and taxable income
Item Impact Reason
Interest on state and local Pretax income > taxable
Interest is tax-free
government bonds income
Fines and penalties Fines are tax-deductible
Taxable income > pretax
Certain entertainment expenses Not all are fully tax-deductible
income
Certain benefits for senior Some benefits, such as company-paid premiums on life insurance,
management are not tax-deductible
Permanent differences between accounting profit (ie, pretax income) and taxable profit (ie, taxable income) arise due to the tax deductibility of
certain items. For example, tax-exempt income from municipal bonds is included in accounting profit and excluded from taxable profit. Since this
difference is not expected to reverse in the future, it is considered permanent.
In contrast, temporary differences between accounting profit and taxable profit arise from the timing of recognizing certain revenues and
expenses. These differences are reflected in deferred tax assets (DTAs) and deferred tax liabilities (DTLs). Since the differences will be reversed
in the future, they are considered temporary (Choice B).
(Choice A) A valuation allowance account is a reserve created to offset deferred tax assets, which capture temporary differences, in the event
that future economic benefits are not realized. In this scenario, the differences between taxable profit and accounting profit are permanent.
